name: Berseem
model: written by hand (Claude) from the Urdu KB

aspects.overview: Berseem (Egyptian clover) is the leading rabi fodder and the most widely grown. As a legume, bacteria in its roots fix nitrogen from the air, keeping the soil fertile. Its fodder has carotene (vitamin A), good for milking animals. With modern practices it gives 40 to 50 tonnes of green fodder per acre. It needs a mild climate; growth slows in severe cold and frost. It can be grown easily in all irrigated areas of Punjab. Heavy loam is best, but it grows on lighter soils too, and on moderately saline land if irrigation is available. Often sown mixed with oats, mustard or ryegrass for an earlier, bigger first cut.
aspects.varieties:
Approved varieties: Chenab Berseem, Punjab Berseem, Agaiti (early) Berseem, Pichheti (late) Berseem, Super Late Faisalabad, Berseem Anmol and Lyallpur Late. Early varieties start giving cuts sooner; late varieties give an extra cut at the end, covering the fodder gap. Anmol and Agaiti Berseem sown on 15 October give about seven cuts up to 31 May. Super Late Faisalabad gives fodder to 31 May and Lyallpur Late to 15 June. Punjab Berseem sown on time gives 7 to 8 cuts and is less affected by stem rot. Choose early or late varieties by your area and fodder needs.
Seed rate: 8 kg per acre. Mixed: with oats 6 kg berseem + 8 to 10 kg oats; with mustard 8 kg berseem + 1 to 2 kg mustard; with ryegrass 7 kg berseem + 1 kg ryegrass per acre.
Bacterial inoculation (rhizobium tika): dissolve 100 g sugar in 1 to 2 litres of water, add one packet of inoculum, mix well with 8 kg seed, dry in shade and sow quickly, as the inoculum weakens over time. Available from the Bacteriology section of Ayub Agricultural Research Institute Faisalabad, NIAB Faisalabad and NARC Islamabad. If no inoculum is available and berseem is new to the field, bring about 2 maunds of soil from last year's berseem field and mix it into one acre.
Seed: use clean, weed-free seed; market seed often contains shaftal, chicory (kasni), riwari and onion-weed seed. If chicory is mixed in, soak seed in a 5 percent salt solution, remove floating seed and wash well. Seed is available from the Punjab Seed Corporation and the fodder research institutes at Sargodha, Bahawalpur and Faisalabad.
aspects.sowing:
Best time: 1 to 15 October, though farmers sow until the end of November. Very early sowing invites weeds, especially swank (sawank) grass; late sowing gives fewer cuts.
Land: plough and plank 3 to 4 times until soft and fine; level well, preferably with a laser land leveller, so water spreads evenly.
Method: broadcast the recommended fertilizer, plough and plank, make basins, irrigate, and broadcast berseem seed into the standing water. In rice areas where the soil doesn't reach workable moisture after the paddy harvest, flood and puddle the field and broadcast the seed.
Mixed with oats: broadcast 8 to 10 kg oats per acre with the fertilizer, plough, plank, make bunds, irrigate, then broadcast 6 kg berseem. With ryegrass: in standing water broadcast berseem first, then ryegrass.
aspects.fertilizer: Get a soil test; for average soil berseem needs 13 kg nitrogen, 35 kg phosphorus and 12 kg potash per acre: 1.5 bags DAP and half a bag of SOP, or 4 bags SSP, half a bag of urea and half a bag of SOP. Nitrogen can be given after each cut as the crop needs; sandy soil needs relatively more fertilizer. If stem rot appears, reduce nitrogen.
aspects.irrigation: Since berseem is sown into standing water, give the first irrigation a week after sowing, then as needed. In severe cold and frost a light irrigation protects the crop. Use canal water where available. Reduce water in February (black spot). In the seed crop water as needed during flowering and pollination. Don't over-water (stem rot).
aspects.pests_diseases:
Diseases:
Stem rot (fungus Sclerotinia trifoliorum): white cottony growth on the lower stems; plants rot and wilt, in patches, usually January–February. Control: deep ploughing, level land, lower seed rate, no over-watering, keep water from diseased fields away from healthy ones, rotate crops, use potash and not too much nitrogen, don't grow host crops nearby. Chemical: after cutting, spray difenoconazole 1.5 ml per litre of water or sulphur 2 g per litre.
Stem/collar canker (fungus): sunken spots on the lower stem, which rots and turns black, then plants dry. Keep fields level so water doesn't stand, don't over-water, don't grow berseem on that field for 3 to 4 years. Chemical: after cutting, spray cymoxanil + mancozeb 2 g per litre or chlorothalonil + metalaxyl-M 2 cc per litre.
Black spot (fungus): dark brown oval spots on leaves and stems; stems rot in severe attack. Water less in February; after cutting spray difenoconazole 1 cc per litre or sulphur 2 g per litre.
Root rot (wilt): plants wilt suddenly, pull out easily, root bark rotten. Treat seed with a recommended fungicide, cut early, don't water without need, don't mix berseem with oats where the disease is expected, rotate, use a lower seed rate, and don't grow berseem for 3 to 4 years where the disease occurred.
Rule: never spray the crop meant for fodder. Spray only seed crops, or spray after cutting the fodder, in the morning or evening to protect bees. Nothing should be sprayed 20 to 25 days before cutting.
Armyworm (lashkari sundi): greenish-brown caterpillar with yellow stripes and two black spots behind the head; curls up when touched. From February–March it eats leaves down to the veins, plus flowers and buds. Don't spray full-grown caterpillars; wait until they pupate. Keep the crop weed-free, use light and sex-pheromone traps, and dig water-filled trenches with kerosene around badly hit fields so caterpillars can't move on. In severe attack, after cutting, spray per acre 50 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml lufenuron.
American bollworm: eats leaves; hay crops suffer most. If essential, cut the fodder and then spray per acre 40 ml spinosad, or 25 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml emamectin benzoate, or 200 ml lufenuron. Use light and pheromone traps; check seed crops and spray while caterpillars are young.
Looper (kubri sundi): green caterpillar that loops when moving; webs and eats tender leaves. Same rules: don't spray fodder, spray after cutting; trenches with kerosene around fields.
Whitefly (seed crop): sucks sap, leaves turn yellow with black sooty mould. Spray per acre 250 ml acetamiprid, or 400 ml flonicamid, or 500 ml pyriproxyfen.
Thrips (seed crop): suck sap so leaves dry. Spray 200 ml chlorfenapyr per acre, and use yellow or blue sticky traps.
Aphid (sust tela): dark green, sucks sap, sooty mould follows. Sow treated seed; never spray the fodder crop. On the seed crop spray per acre 200 ml imidacloprid or nitenpyram, or 250 ml acetamiprid or bifenthrin.
Shoot fly: enters and dries the shoots; in severe attack cut the fodder, then spray 200 ml imidacloprid or emamectin benzoate per acre.
Fodder weevil: larva and adult eat green leaf tissue and new shoots; cut the fodder early. On the seed crop spray 40 to 50 ml flubendiamide or chlorantraniliprole per acre.
Lygus and sting bugs: damage buds, flowers and green pods so flowers drop and seed shrivels, mostly in the seed crop. Spray a recommended insecticide.
aspects.weeds:
Frequent cutting helps control weeds; rotate with other rabi crops. Very early sowing increases weeds such as swank grass.
Itsit: spray pendimethalin 1.5 litres per acre three weeks to a month before sowing and irrigate; plough at wattar and leave open.
Ghabbal grass: spray quizalofop 350 to 400 ml per acre.
Do not hoe right after spraying: dust can carry the chemical into the farmer's body.
aspects.harvesting:
Fodder: first cut in December, last cut in April (late varieties to May–June). For hay, cut at about 10 percent flowering. No spray of any kind 20 to 25 days before cutting.
Seed: after 3 to 4 fodder cuts, leave early varieties for seed at the end of March and late varieties in the first week of April. Seed yield is 10 to 15 maunds per acre in good weather. Beehives near large seed fields improve pollination. Harvest when fully ripe (green pods give immature seed), in the morning or evening so ripe pods don't drop. Stack the cut crop in the field and thresh with a thresher when dry; on large areas use a combine harvester. Store seed in a dry, airy store.
aspects.machinery: Laser land leveller for levelling; thresher or combine harvester for the seed crop.
aspects.other: Mixed sowing with oats, mustard or ryegrass gives an earlier first cut and more fodder.

timing.sowing: 1 October to 15 October (up to end of November)
timing.harvesting: first cut December, last cut April (late varieties to May–June)
